utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness today is Colonel Stewart; he's here and ready to go. He would obviously like to be finished today, if at all possible. We have not yet had from Trial Chamber I an order releasing the document that I've referred to on earlier occasions, and therefore I haven't been able to show the document to this witness for his comments. I'm hopeful that in the course of the morning there may be notification from Trial Chamber I that the document can be released. If it is released, I'd ask for the witness to have a short adjournment at a convenient time to consider the document, and I'd ask to be allowed to speak to him if there's anything he wants to say about it, but of course limited to that document and nothing else at that stage as he will have already started to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, before we do, there are various formal matters. The first is this, that there are only two Judges sitting today, Judge Robinson being away, as is known, for urgent personal reasons. We propose, therefore, to make a further order under Rule 15 bis because we regard it in the interests of justice to get on with this case and to hear this evidence, the witness being here or witnesses being here this week. We propose to make the order for three days, as the Rule provides, unless anybody has any submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Other than what we've said earlier, we have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. I take that to be a reference to the amount of reading for Judge Robinson. It is something which we covered or I covered in my conversation with him which I referred to last week. Accordingly, we'll make the order in the interests of justice under Rule 15 bis. The next matter is this, that we have had the transcript of Colonel Stewart's evidence in Blaskic. It's evidence which was given under oath and subject to cross-examination, and we would propose that it be made an exhibit in this case so that it's part of the record. Is there any objection to that course?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacic. I didn't ask you about the Rule 15 bis order. Since the transcript was part or is part of the record and since we've had the opportunity of reading it, it would be sufficient for counsel to refer to passages in it on which they rely. There are more references, I note, to Mr. Kordic, for instance, than appear in your summary, one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But albeit, if the same points are to be made, then a reference to the transcript would be sufficient rather than taking the witness all the way through it again, saying, "Do you agree," and of course, he will say, "Yes, I agree with what I said on oath three months ago," or "six months ago," and I hope in that way we can speed things up. You anticipated you would be about an hour, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Probably less. It really would be in everybody's interests so we can get through the work this week and also so that the witness himself can get away if we can conclude his cross-examination today. I hope that's going to be possible. If there are references to the witness's book and his diary, again if counsel want to rely on parts of it, there's no need to go over it all, we can be referred to it and we can read it at our leisure. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps just a technical question for later work. Since the transcript of this witness from his testimony in the other case will be somehow, how should I say it, I'm missing the technical word, tender it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Part of the record. It will be part of the record in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But should it then have a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it probably should have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we know how to handle it technically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. A Prosecution Exhibit, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we think of the appropriate number to give it, given that we've been attaching numbers with significance. We'll try and find an appropriate number. Maybe transcripts should start a new series at a high number, but I'll think of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you will deal with that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Robert Alexander Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have to leave a gap between questions and answers to allow for simultaneous translation to take place, or translation to take place. Colonel Stewart, were you commanding officer of the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment in Bosnia October 1992 to May 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed now the witness statement you gave, as well as the testimony you gave in the Blaskic case? Do you have any comments to make by way of correction of either of those documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I have reviewed the documents and I have no amendments or adjustments to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly how many times did you meet Dario Kordic in the course of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think about four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just confirm that you've seen a summary of your evidence today? Indeed, it may be before you at the moment. Is that summary something with which you also agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although it may be before you, if you would be so good as to try and speak directly to the Judges on questions, using, as it were, the words that come to you today, I would be grateful, to give vitality to your evidence. In forming conclusions about Kordic, I want to check that we've listed the sources of information available to you. Did those sources include the personal encounters with Kordic himself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, they did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The system of reporting from your patrols, how did that information reach you; directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It reached me directly, and often I formed my own conclusions because I was out on patrol a lot, and so there were various sources of information that reached me as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before information reached you, did it pass through an intelligence officer or a system of intelligence handling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The answer to that question is it depended. It depended -- if it was considered to be vital, it would come direct to me, unfiltered. But the normal system was that all patrols were briefed and debriefed both before -- they were briefed before they went on patrol and they were debriefed on return from patrol by what I call the intelligence section and by the briefers in the intelligence section.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also receive information from ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were quite useful, because they used to operate in areas that I didn't necessarily patrol, and the reason why they would operate in areas I didn't necessarily patrol was because they generally operated in the more passive areas, whereas I wanted to concentrate my efforts in the areas where there was more trouble, indeed where the ECMM, who were unarmed and unprotected by armour, could not operate, except sometimes I lent them armour that I -- from my own resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive information or intelligence from locally-employed staff, including interpreters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, but in many ways the information I received from the interpreters was gained by the fact that they were with me or with our patrols when we were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive information direct from the HVO and from the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but we made sure, as a principle, that we didn't pass on information we received from the HVO, the BiH, to the opposition. It was one of the unwritten rules that I laid down, that we would not pass information given to us by one side to the other. Otherwise, of course, one, we would be distrusted sometimes more than we were before, and equally I didn't think that was proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, did you receive information directly from local inhabitants to whom you or perhaps others but you certainly spoke?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: This was the most important source of information. As I was on the ground quite a lot, what someone who lived in a house that I visited told me must have been the most important raw data. The fact that someone who lived there all his life was telling me something gave it the greatest credibility. So in my view, receiving information direct from the people that lived on the ground, whether they be Bosnian Croats or Bosnian Muslims, was the most important and crucial information I was to receive, and for that reason and that reason chiefly, I spent a lot of my time actually talking to people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have, please, the map 2781,2 for reference as he may decide. If it can be left on the ELMO, I expect Colonel Stewart knows how to use it, from his evidence in the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've listed, Colonel Stewart, personal encounters with Kordic to which you attach particular significance, and in relation to each of those, I'd like you, please, to summarise, in a couple of sentences, what happened, and then to say what conclusion you draw from it. First, was there an incident at Novi Travnik on the 20th of October of 1992 that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This was at a time when my battalion was not in theatre. It was during the reconnaissance, when we were deciding how and where we would actually position my troops in Central Bosnia. I was on my own, insofar as I had a maximum of about 20 people with me. We were based in the school in Vitez, which was empty, actually using the gymnasium to sleep in there, and what happened on the 20th of October was that there was serious fighting which had erupted in Vitez and the surrounding area. It was so serious that I thought it would terminate -- could possibly terminate the deployment of United Nations troops into Central Bosnia, which of course would destroy the mission I had been given. For that reason, I took immediate action to try and sort the problem. I remember that on the 20th, I went into the Hotel Vitez, which I had stayed at previously, to try and find who was in charge. I was told by the commander there that the reason why there was fighting and the reason why there were roadblocks was because the Muslims were causing trouble. In fact, there was some shooting around the Vitez Hotel, which was the HVO headquarters as well. And having done that, I was told I ought to go and see the Bosnian Muslim commander, which I did. He was in a school, and I remember he was sitting, when I went in to see him, in the sort of headmaster's office, and the window was smashed, the result of an RPG 7 or anti-tank missile hitting just below the window, so which had smashed all the glass. He said that had happened during the night. Anyway, on return to the Hotel Vitez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, forgive me. Let me interrupt you, because there's something which I would like clarified. You were told to go and see the Bosnian Muslim commander, and you did so, and you saw him in the school. That I take it to be in Vitez. Who was that, please, if you remember? If you don't remember, just say so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I do remember. A guy called Sefkija. That's the way I wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: And I was sent to that area by Cerkez, the HVO commander, as he said, in Vitez. Anyway, I saw Sefkija. I returned to the hotel. It wasn't particularly easy because there was a heck of a lot of shooting, but we didn't come under fire. Then I went to Novi Travnik, which was extremely difficult, and something like in the afternoon I set up a convoy and went to Novi Travnik, got stopped at a roadblock outside Novi Travnik by an HVO -- by HVO personnel, and then drove into Travnik. It was, to say the least, extremely hazardous. We were driving Land Rovers, and it seemed to me like we were walking into an ambush. I don't know why none of my vehicles were hit. And we careered through Novi Travnik, going initially to find the BiH headquarters, apparently commanded by a man called Lendo. I spoke to Lendo when we got there, an unpleasant man, and told him that the fighting had to stop. And apparently he had some prisoners or hostages. I demanded that he give them to me immediately. He refused. I said I wasn't prepared to have a refusal, but he still refused. Then as I was about to leave, he produced one man. This man was terrified. In fact, as I recall, he didn't seem to have the basics. He had a shirt on and he probably had -- you know, I had the impression of shoes without laces and things like that. But he was clearly a very frightened individual. Anyway, I thought one was better than none, and I told Lendo that the fighting had to stop, that it was disgraceful, and to that end I was going to go to the HVO headquarters. Once I got some sense out of the so-called HVO hostage, once he stopped being so frightened, he agreed to direct me to the HVO headquarters. There was still some firing as we crossed town and we went to a place which I think was called the Cafe Grand, and inside the Cafe Grand I met Kordic for the first time. It was an upstairs bar in the Cafe Grand, and again my task, as I saw it, was to try and get both the HVO and the BiH to stop fighting. In answer to the question finally, and I'm sorry it's taken so long to get there, that is the first time I met Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was he dressed? Was he alone? If not, what sort of people were with him? In a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He was dressed in military fatigues without insignia; in fact, the HVO didn't seem to carry insignia at the time. He was surrounded by people who were similarly dressed and he appeared to be the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he speak to you and negotiate with you as the commander or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he or did anybody else identify any senior HVO commander in Novi Travnik to whom you should have referred at that stage, or were matters conducted on the basis that Kordic was in charge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I went there expecting to find Blaskic and so I was somewhat surprised when Kordic was there but Blaskic was not, because one of the reasons I had come to Novi Travnik was also to speak to Blaskic. Blaskic wasn't there but Kordic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion that Kordic was deferring to Blaskic or that you would have to refer to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, there was not. In fact, the fact of the matter was I didn't really contemplate the matter at all because as far as I was concerned I had one urgent overriding priority, that was to stop the fighting, and I'd deal with anyone who could help do that, and Kordic appeared to be the man in charge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to the next incident, but we'll take "C" ahead of "B" because I think this may fit chronologically. In summary, was there an incident involving a Danish soldier kidnapped by the HVO in respect of whom the United Nations had been asked for help?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, there was. At one stage, the Danish contingent in Kiseljak had apparently lost a soldier who had been along the road, on his own, I think, and he was kidnapped. The fact of the matter was I knew Dario Kordic. I was telephoned from Kiseljak by the United Nations command and asked if I could help to get this soldier freed. In fact, I'd had dinner with Dario Kordic either the night before or the night before that in my headquarters, along with the commanders of the BiH, a dinner night as we call them, and I sent Captain Martin Foregrave to see Dario Kordic to ask if he could use his influence to get this soldier released. Apparently it had some influence because the soldier was released four hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to subparagraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can we establish a date for this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to establish a date for this, Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But where do you believe it to fit in relation to the next incident which I was going to deal with, the 4th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So dealing with the 4th of February in Busovaca at the PTT building, and referring to the map if that's going to assist us, tell us what happened and what significance you saw in it particularly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I visited the PTT building in Busovaca on the 4th of February. Kordic was by that time the military commander of Busovaca, as I recall, still not wearing military rank but certainly wearing military fatigues. He was quite agitated, which I thought was unusual. He was agitated, I felt, because of the advance of the BiH across the hills towards Busovaca. He asked me to do all I could to stop the fighting, which I took to be a sign that actually the HVO might be losing this particular matter. I think on that date I went into the area of Katici and also -- it doesn't show on your map, it has to be opened out. It's still not helpful. Can I have it? Just to orientate, Vitez is there [indicates]; Busovaca is here. This road is the valley road along the Lasva Valley that goes round to Zenica. This junction here [indicates], the T-junction is strategically important because this is the dividing line between going to Zenica and going down to Kiseljak, and Busovaca stood here [indicates]. The PTT building was obviously in the centre of Busovaca. I visited the PTT building here [indicates] and was told the fighting was enormous around up here [indicates], and could I help. I went to Katici and Medani in my armoured vehicle, and I think it was getting dark at the time. Again, this was a serious area of confrontation and we came under fire when we did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, over all, did this encounter with the agitated Dario Kordic show you about military command in him at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: My conclusion was that Kordic had decided or had been put in charge of Busovaca from his position as the political director to try and get a control over the situation there, and my conclusion was, and I'm sure of this, that at the time he was the HVO commander in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn to the 22nd of February. Was there an incident there involving a roadblock on the Zenica road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I had negotiated that this roadblock, which, if you look at the map, would of course be a big problem, it was somewhere near here [indicates] where the main road came close to the river, and there was a cliff and the cliff had been brought down to effectively block the road with explosives -- it had been brought down by explosives to block the road. If you can imagine, there were only two routes into Zenica; one, the easiest route along the main road and the other, the valley route where there were frequent roadblocks and where there was an area of confrontation. To actually lose the easy access to Zenica where all the international agencies tend to have their headquarters and their control points was a blow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said the alternative was the valley road. Did you mean the alternative was the mountain road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Forgive me, I meant the mountain road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll be looking at that in a few minutes, so press on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: So I was very concerned to get this roadblock removed, and I remember one of my company commanders, a Major Jennings, was tasked by me to get it fixed. He didn't really manage that, and so I put a lot of effort into getting it removed. I spoke to Blaskic and he agreed that the route could be opened. When I visited Kordic, he didn't agree that the route could be opened and said that Blaskic's word on this did not matter, it was not to be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it opened or did it remain --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, it wasn't opened then. It took a few more days and required me to guarantee that I would provide security on that route by having a checkpoint of my soldiers permanently established there. This was something I really loathed doing. I did not like establishing checkpoints because it -- well, it sort of implicated a lot of my soldiers in static duties and took a lot of manpower, and frankly I didn't think it was particularly effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence already and, indeed, seen film already of your discovery of the massacre at Ahmici. That's been dealt with also in your testimony in the Blaskic case, and I'm not going to take you through it at all. But did you, after that discovery on the 26th of April, have an encounter with Kordic, where he gave an explanation to you for what had happened at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Kordic told me that the incident at Ahmici had been caused by Bosnian Serbs seeking to kill Muslims and blame the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your response at the time to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I thought it was laughable and pathetic and obviously was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you tell him as much?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn now to your conclusions from all the sources of information about Kordic. How connected was he to the top of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He was definitely connected to the top of the HVO, as he told me himself. He was the Deputy President, a political Deputy President or Vice-President. He was proud of that, and he was primarily, in my view, a political leader in Central Bosnia, political in the sense, I have to add, in the sense of giving direction to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll return to that conclusion a little further on but deal with some detailed matters first. How connected to Valenta?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: My impression was that Valenta was almost his professor, almost someone from whom he derived inspiration or -- Valenta had written a book. I never read it because, of course, I can't read Croatian. But when he explained it to me verbally, it seemed to me rather like Mein Kampf, insofar as Mein Kampf suggested ethnic cleansing and so too did Valenta's book, apparently, from what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subparagraph (D), because we've dealt with (C). As things developed, did you judge whether Kordic's involvement in military affairs was constant or diminished or grew? Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The answer is he started as a political controller, although the incident on the 20th of October, 1992, seemed to demonstrate that he was a decision-maker too in the military, you know, with regard to the Novi Travnik business. But he got increasingly involved in the military situation, witnessed by the fact that by the end of my time in Bosnia, he was the commander in Busovaca. He most certainly was not a military officer by profession, Blaskic was, an ex-JNA officer who had personal knowledge and, I suspect, some liking for people like Merdan in the BiH, as Kordic's background tended to be as a journalist and also someone politically involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see some indication, from individual members of the HVO, how they regarded Kordic's military abilities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the HVO soldiers who were doing the fighting often didn't have much time for Kordic and considered him inept in terms of being a military commander. "Laugh behind their hands" would be an English way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did that necessarily find reflection in their refusing to honour or to obey any orders that may have come from or via him or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so. It was just an aside that I felt. I mean the situation was always confusing. My view was that Blaskic was the military commander and Kordic was the political commander. As someone that has studied the Soviet armed forces for most of my time in the British army, there was no surprise that the opponents in the Balkans would be organised along the kind of Soviet-type principle whereby there was a military commander and a political commander side by side. That was how the JNA was organised, you know, initially along Soviet lines before the split with Tito, but probably continued. And so therefore the experience of people who had been in the armed forces was that these two political/military commanders would work side by side and that in normal times the military commander would have to get the agreement of the political commander to do anything. And so my view was and remains that Blaskic was the appointed military commander for Central Bosnia and that Kordic was the appointed political commander for Central Bosnia. But remember, when you say "appointed", this was the HVO at a time when it was forming itself. You know, I have sympathy for the fact that, you know, all these things were being done at great speed, so it wasn't, you know, as if they had manuals and books and standard operational procedures. It was done really, you know, as needs must.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've dealt effectively with subparagraphs (E), his influence at the negotiations in October 1992, (F), his military command in Busovaca in 1993. (G), you've really dealt with his status vis-a-vis Blaskic and the fact that he countermanded on overruled Blaskic on the 22nd of February. I turn to (H). Did you ever see Kordic personally involved in war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I never did, and I think that's fair. I never did that, and neither did I have the impression that he had personally been involved in war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the Ahmici attack, what amplification from what's in your summary -- by the time of the Ahmici attack, was there any evidence available to you of the developing situation and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Ahmici occurred on the 16th of April, 1993. It was clear to me that the situation in Central Bosnia had been deteriorating for some time with regard to the relationship between the HVO and BiH. The attack on Ahmici must have been pre-planned. You know, as an experienced military officer, you don't assemble the number of troops to do that kind of operation without some pre-planning, and therefore the attack on Ahmici must have been known and condoned -- I mean agreed to by Mr. Kordic, because he was still at that time the political -- dare I use the word -- commissar for Central Bosnia. I cannot see Blaskic or anyone else involved in this operation carrying out such a disgusting crime without political agreement. Political agreement in Central Bosnia came through Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally and more generally on this topic, any other policies that the Chamber may find existed about, for example, ethnic cleansing generally, to what degree must they, in your judgement, have involved political approval or contribution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that the decisions on ethnic cleansing stemmed from two sources. One was the political strategy of the HVO, led by people like Ante Valenta, and as I previously said, Kordic seemed to be a disciple of these thoughts. And the other catalyst, I'm afraid to say, was the suggestion that the area of Central Bosnia would be divided under the Vance-Owen Plan into certain areas which seemed to be rather absurd. For example, Gornji Vakuf, largely Muslim, was given to the Croats, and Novi Travnik, very much Muslim, was given also to the Croats, and the Croats were meant to sort of centralise in Zenica. One of the reasons I think why the trouble that had been brewing for some time started was to quickly expedite this so-called political solution so that people could, de facto, change the situation before the International Community realised they got it wrong, the International Community represented by Vance-Owen. But fundamentally, any ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia must have been agreed to by the political leadership of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so the setup, as you saw it, was that one where political controllers could overrule military commanders or where military commanders could overrule political commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the leading nature of that question, You Honour, and to the extent that it calls for speculation and conjecture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it is leading. It is open-ended, because it wants an "either/or" answer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The answer is that I felt that political always led.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any example of Kordic's orders being overruled either by the military or by anybody further up any political or military chain and therefore superior to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know from other evidence that you required investigation into Ahmici from Blaskic. At the time you made that requirement and based on your experience as a soldier, would written documents have existed or not to show what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that there would have been written orders to prepare for the attack on Ahmici. I suspect there may have been a written debrief for what happened at Ahmici. But most clearly, because of the disgusting, disgraceful situation that happened in Ahmici and elsewhere, such documents would have been suppressed or destroyed, because they were like political dynamite. I want to say one more thing at this stage. There were -- I found evidence that there were also crimes against humanity perpetrated by the BiH, but not, in my area, at least, in any way like the scale of those that normally occurred in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was any report or were any raw documents ever produced to you by Blaskic or anyone else in defence of the various positions they took to explain Ahmici and to explain why the HVO weren't involved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, there was an answer to the letter I sent immediately after I discovered Ahmici, sent to me by Blaskic. I saw it in the Blaskic trial. I'm quite sure and I'm perfectly willing to accept it came. I'm not willing to accept, though, that anything was done in my time, and I departed from Central Bosnia on the 10th of May, 1993, that there was absolutely nothing done to investigate openly, with access to anyone, what had happened at the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see, in order to refresh the Tribunal's recollection, D64/1, as the document, I think, to which he is referring. If we can lay that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that the document you had in mind when you say that there was a reply shown to you in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will have read it before and there's no need to reread it. May we go into private session just briefly because of the sensitivity of another potential witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And would the Chamber have to look at but not to lay on the ELMO document 887.2. I'm so sorry. I was going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're now in public session, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I know what the difference between private and public session is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session is that nothing is heard by the public gallery, so that what you say can't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But in private session, what I say can still get out of this court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court has powers to control the dissemination of information and the Defence counsel are under duties to not disseminate publicly what is revealed only privately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What about the defendant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to know this, sir, because, you know, I'm talking about something that matters very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's a matter which troubles you about this, we'll give you leave to talk to Mr. Nice during the adjournment about it and then it can be explained to you, and if there is a matter which should be drawn to the attention of the Court, we'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I answer, it's nothing suspicious. It's just that general military practice in the British army does not necessarily identify people who work for special operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course not. But, as I say, if you would like to have a word with Mr. Nice about it, it can either be cleared up or we'll make some sort of order if we need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't need to, sir, but I just wanted to be clear on that because I'm concerned, because normal practice is that we don't identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the map to hand and bearing in mind that the learned Judges haven't visited the area, can you just explain a little more about the mountain road, you might want to unwrap it, unfold the map, and show us the utility to you of the mountain road in contrast with the valley road.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: If I can orientate you again, Vitez is here [indicates], there; there is Zenica [indicates] where the international agencies tended to be based; here [indicates] is my military headquarters where I tended to be based. The only two routes to Zenica were as follows: the valley route which went down the Lasva Valley to a junction here [indicates], this road went to Sarajevo; and if you turned left or kept going, you went into Zenica. A good well-maintained acceptable road for the deployment of logistic transport and humanitarian aid, obviously. The valley road was the best route for getting heavy vehicles into Zenica. The alternative route was what we always called the mountain road which went high up to this point, the highest point, and then all the way down this valley into Zenica. This was obviously quicker as a bird would fly, but this may well have been quicker by virtue of the ease of transport, you didn't have to climb. Personally, I would generally use the mountain road if I was in a Discovery Land Rover and the valley road if I was in an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How frequently or otherwise did you use the mountain road? What about at the time of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: At the time of Ahmici, on the 16th of April, I probably went in three times to Zenica in that day -- at least two, probably three times. You have to recall that my diary was written the next day and I didn't necessarily -- I was tired and I just sort of bounced around and put down most things, but it wasn't a blow-by-blow account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To make sense of that and to connect it to what the Chamber's dealing with, you've been asked about and do you have any recollection of any incident where you were given assistance with the moving of mines on the road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, sometimes people would help me move mines on the road, any road, and sometimes I'd do it on my own. Obviously we learnt relatively quickly, we hoped, that all the mines were not -- the anti-tank mines, vehicle mines, were not booby-trapped. They generally were movable. In fact, I don't think I can recall an instance even with so-called tilt switches, which is rods on top of anti-tank mines, that they were booby-trapped, which was normal custom in a professional armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up your evidence of a couple of answers ago, you've looked at your diary in relation to, as it were, day return trips over the mountain road to Zenica, you've dealt with the 16th of April. Does your diary allow the possibility of any day return trip to Zenica on the 15th or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: On the 15th I went to Zenica but I didn't return. I was summoned by --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again, that's all we need. If you went there and you didn't return, then it wasn't a day return trip?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The 14th, no. I was in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the 15th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The 15th I spent the morning in my headquarters dealing with paperwork. In the early afternoon I was in Novi Travnik until I was summoned to go to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you regularly enough pick up people that you met on the roads whether or not that accorded with policy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Sir, the official policy was that we were not to take people on board our vehicles, but the official policy was nonsense when I considered there to be a threat to the people, and so I countermanded that order, which is a United Nation's order, and gave instructions to my soldiers that where people's lives were at risk or they considered it to be a humanitarian purpose, i.e., someone who needed to go to hospital or even a soldier, I didn't consider that a soldier wasn't human, if a soldier was wounded and we could help him by saving his life, we were to do so. So the answer to the question, I'm sorry I put that in context, the answer to the question is I would willingly pick up people who I felt there was a need to give them a lift, whether they be Muslim, Croat, or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Two other matters of detail and then I'm done. First, and again this is not covered in your summary but I think you may want to make reference to it, you saw one or more than one places used as prisons in the area of Busovaca or Busovaca/Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, in the area of Busovaca, two; one I call Kaonik and another one which is unnamed but to the south of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any significance to the fact that there were two places used as prisons in the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think it was convenience more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then one document only to look at, please. It's Exhibit Z306 coming up. This is a milinfosum, the 6th of December of 1992, and it's the passage at the foot of the first page where there's a reference to the man called Marinko, did you know the man called Marinko?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I might have done, but I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that as reported, Marinko stated that he knew Kordic well and described Blaskic and Kordic at that time, the end of December or the beginning of December, as two bodies, one mind, claiming that Novi Travnik was a Croat town and would form part of the new State of Herceg-Bosna, being happy that Muslims should leave for, say, Zenica. How did that expression of views fit or otherwise with your understanding of the position at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I mean this is what I understood to be accurate. I think this is something that comes from Valenta's book, and I think this information was probably gathered by one of my liaison officers. I personally didn't have either knowledge or input to this military information summary. It was done normally by the staff, and normally I didn't have an input unless I told them to put something into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, subject to the matter that may arise if we have an appropriate order from the other Trial Chamber, that's all I ask of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning, Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My name is Steve Sayers. I'm one of the attorneys representing Dario Kordic in this case. Behind me are Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Mikulicic, and they represent Mario Cerkez. The questions that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just ask, Mario Cerkez is not on trial here, it's just Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez is on trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two accused.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: There are two accused here, same trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two accused here. I'm sorry you weren't told about that. Both in the same trial, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought he was, and indeed I realise I omitted to deal with paragraph 9, which I would have wanted to have dealt with, but it can be dealt with, because it's all favourable, in a sense, it can be dealt with now or in cross-examination later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can read paragraph 9. No doubt Mr. Kovacic can ask some questions about it, if he wants. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, for your purposes and for the Trial Chamber's purposes, let me just say that I propose to ask you three broad areas of questions. I hope to be complete by today, but that depends on the kind of progress that we make. First, I want to ask you some general questions about the diaries or the diary that you maintained and the book you wrote, some general questions on the HVO chain of command. I will also ask you about a couple of other subjects on a general matter. Secondly, I would like to take you through, carefully and chronologically, the events in which you have personal knowledge and about which you've given some testimony today, and that's going to be the largest part of the cross-examination. Finally, I'll ask you some questions in connection with the Ahmici opinions that you've given today. And I'll try to do my best to let you know when the break is so that you can prepare yourself for that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's very decent of you. That's very much. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you've made two preliminary visits in the nature of reconnaissance visits to Bosnia-Herzegovina before actually leading your regiment or the 1st Battalion of your regiment to their tour of duty in Central Bosnia. The first reconnaissance visit was at the end of September; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you very briefly visited the town of Vitez at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Umm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that "yes"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Yes, I did. It lasted two weeks, actually. I spent some time in Serbia as well, one week in Serbia and one week in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Most of your visit, though, was spent in the Tuzla region, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: In the first instance, my -- most of my visit in Serbia was spent trying to get to Tuzla. I never got there. I got stuck in around the area of Zvornik. And when I was in Central Bosnia, I did get to Tuzla from the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then your second visit lasted from, I believe, October the 18th to October the 22nd, when you flew back to Split; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure, without reference to -- but the answer is, yes, it sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Blaskic case that you were instructed to keep a contemporaneous diary from Lieutenant General Sir Jeromy McKenzie. I would just like to show you a copy of the diary you maintained, and we'll have it marked as an exhibit, with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D151/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The document that was marked D151/1 and which I've just had the registrar put in front of you is an accurate copy of the contemporaneous diary that you maintained; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it looks it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, if you just keep that by you, we'll be referring to that occasionally during the course of your cross-examination. The second document I would like to show you is a completely separate document entitled "The Commander's Diary, 1 Cheshire," and I believe this is the official battalion war diary, and I would just like you to identify this for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D152/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, the document that we've just shown you is the official diary of significant events that was maintained by the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. This is done by my second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's in the nature of an official record, if you like, of the doings of the battalion during their tour of duty in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: As he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As he saw it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: As he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And your second in command initially, I believe, was Major Tim Park. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, until Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was replaced then by Major Brian Watters or then Major Brian Watters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Finally along these lines, Colonel, you were requested by the British army to write a book about your experiences in Central Bosnia, and that book was published, I believe, by Harper Collins in 1993 and entitled "Broken Lives." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It was the director of public relations, army, that actually suggested I write a book and told me to go to an agent, and the reason why he did that was because he said that it would make absolute sense to do so and it would stop people pushing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the book obviously was written in the same year as your tour of duty; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just have the registrar mark the various portions of the book to which we'll be referring during this cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D153/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. Let's just start with the book "Broken Lives." That's your picture on the front, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to make much progress if we ask that sort of question. It's obviously his picture. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You opine, sir, on page 319 of the book, that Bosnia was undergoing a classic civil war fought by civilians against civilians; a civilian one minute is a soldier the next. I take it, sir, that you still agree with that overall view of the situation that confronted you and which you endured, actually, throughout your tour of duty in Central Bosnia in the first half of 1993 and the latter two months or the latter month -- two months, I suppose, of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In addition, you relate, on page 19 of the book, in connection with the initial briefings that you were given to prepare you to lead your men into Central Bosnia, sir, that Sir Peter Inge told you on September the 13th that the hatred generated between the opposing factions was almost impossible to believe. Do you recall that briefing that you were given by --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think Inge had been to Sarajevo before that, and I do recall him telling me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In addition, sir, just the final question along these lines, on page 6 you relate that, historically, relations between Serbs, Croats and Muslims had been appalling for centuries; rivalries between each group had frequently led to wars and massacres; the place has always been considered a powder keg. I believe that that's essentially the briefing that you received to prepare you for your duties. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, not the briefing that you received but some of the information that was communicated to you as background; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It was about all I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you knew nothing about the Balkans before your posting to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Beyond where they were and a bit of history, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In connection with the intelligence section that you've described in your direct examination, Colonel, that's what you called the milinfocell or military information cell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The United Nations initially told me that there was no such thing as intelligence for a United Nations operation, and I said that I disagreed with that. I think they called -- they told me to call it the information room. I refused to do such a thing. I said intelligence is required in order to operate as a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your intelligence section, I believe, was under the command of Captain Christopher Leyshon.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you always found him to be a reliable and trustworthy and effective young officer, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He was effective enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard a lot of information already, Colonel, about military information summaries or milinfosums and the military information cell generally, but it's true, is it not, that the task of the intelligence section was to prepare contemporaneous reports and summaries of significant happenings and events in your area of operations, your AOR?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. The task of an intelligence cell is to prepare the soldiers that go on the ground to do their job and take information from -- which they receive on that patrol and investigate, collate it, so that actually we are more effective next time we go on. As part of its responsibilities, it has a reporting duty as well, but the primary task of an intelligence organisation is to assist those people that go on the ground. And while we're on that subject, just because an intelligence cell produces an assessment doesn't necessarily mean that people like myself read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, Colonel, but I'm just trying to get an idea of how the information is put together.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was an aside. I'll answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that the commander would generally hold a briefing every day, and this would be attended by the representatives of the milinfocell as well as by the liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It not only was general, it happened at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you reported, you yourself and your liaison officers, reported the results of their investigation each day; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The staff reported the investigations. I didn't necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You felt that your liaison officers, for example, Captain Foregrave or Captain Dundas-Whatley, were effective, and you had a high opinion of their operational efficiency during your tour of duty; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that question in the book, I would say they were great, but when I actually assessed them as individuals, I might give a different answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just before you visited Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were actually given some background information about what you could expect to find from Lieutenant Colonel Colin Doyle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he told you, and this is recorded, I believe, on pages 29 and 30 of your book and also on page 280 of your book, and it's also recorded in your diary, sir, on September 25th of 1992, that Lieutenant Colonel Doyle told you that you should be very careful to ascertain the truth, because all people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were really good at twisting it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, he instructed you that all parties were quite prepared to attack their own people and to blame it on someone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He told me that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, it was your experience that it was absolutely routine for the warring parties to point fingers at one another when incidents occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions, Colonel, on the HVO chain of command. You knew that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on to another topic, I think that would be a convenient moment for our break. Mr. Nice, if you make your application to speak to the witness, would you want to do that over the longer adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any order coming from Trial Chamber I in relation to the other matter. I'll check with the witness whether he wants to say anything, but I think his last answer was that he didn't need to say anything else. But I'll have a word with him, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may to ensure that nothing else is to be added. But in due course you're going to make an application in relation to the document if it comes from Trial Chamber I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can do that before the longer adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, just before the break, I told you that we were going to go over the chain of command within the HVO, and I would like to address that in a fairly summary way right now. These questions should be fairly simple. If you need to expand on any answer, just let me know. First, you knew that the headquarters of the HVO general staff was in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that the commander in chief of the HVO armed forces was Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The military command of the HVO was actually divided into various so-called operative zones; for example, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone under the command of Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and the Northwest Herzegovina Operative Zone under the command, at least during your tour of duty, of commander Zeljko Siljeg; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Each of these operative zones was commanded by a separate commander who in turn reported to the commander in chief of the general staff in Mostar, Brigadier Petkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And insofar as the operative zones were concerned, Colonel, they were actually divided into municipality-based brigades; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: If you want to call them brigades, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. To the extent that they were brigades, there was a brigade, for example, located in Vitez, one in Novi Travnik, and another in Busovaca, just as examples; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: As examples, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Each of the brigades was commanded by a brigade commander who in turn reported to the operative zone commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: As far as we could see it. Can I just -- it was not -- we never had an order of battle laid down, this was supposition as we determined it, and neither were we indiscrete enough to ask exactly what it was, indiscrete, I mean, from the point of view that I thought it was inappropriate to ask such questions and make suppositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So you never obviously asked Colonel Blaskic what the relationship with Mr. Kordic was insofar as the military chain of command was concerned, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. I think I might have done actually because I didn't totally comprehend -- it wasn't clear-cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think I might have done, but I don't think it's recorded in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You knew that, for example, Colonel Blaskic had the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca under his command, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You knew that he had the ability to issue orders to the 4th Battalion of the military police headquartered in Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, he had under his command so-called special purpose units, such as the Vitezovi under the command of Darko Kraljevic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You do not. Very well. Now, you testified in the Blaskic case that there could have been a political and a military chain of command, that there was suspicions along those lines, but that the British remained confused as to the chain of command and never actually confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber's purposes, I merely refer to pages 23764 and 23749.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's still your impression today, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never once claimed to you that there was any duality in the chain of command whatsoever, did he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never once claimed to me that there was duality and there was duality in the chain of command, that is correct. Sorry, I am just rehearsing the question again, just so I'm clear. No, I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you never raised the subject with Mr. Kordic as to whether he had any military authority at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same is true with respect to any other Bosnian Croat leader to whom you spoke, including Brigadier Petkovic and Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, no, I think I might have talked to Blaskic about it actually, you know, because he was -- no, I think I might have done but I can't say it's fact. I've got this impression I might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, there was no doubt in your mind, and I think you've said this in your direct examination and you certainly said it in the Blaskic case but I'd just like to ask you one question on this, there's no doubt in your mind that Colonel Blaskic was the military commander of the HVO armed forces in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He said he was; I accepted that; he seemed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you always considered him to be the commander, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe you told Judge Shahabuddeen, on page 8355, that in your opinion Colonel Blaskic was the real commander of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia and you never thought of Mr. Kordic as the commander and never referred to him as the commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, too, except with the Busovaca thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever tell anybody that you considered Mr. Kordic to be the military commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think I have said -- yes, I think I have said that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know. It's generally -- it's what appeared in my diary, what I appeared -- it appeared correct at the time. And remember, going to the evidence I've already given this morning, that Mr. Kordic did appear to have the military command decision-making in Novi Travnik on the 20th of October, although I didn't think that was permanent. But I did think that he was commander in Busovaca, correct, and I don't know -- I've said that openly, so I don't know who I've said it to. Lots of people, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you inform your military intelligence section of that opinion, sir, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think they knew about it. I mean sometimes I would walk down and debrief -- be debriefed so that we had a record of it, but to be quite honest, I didn't have very much time on my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Stewart, sorry to interrupt you, but I have to ask if Colonel Kordic had the command over the Busovaca area, would that appear in military documents such as orders, for example, or would that become transparent in military type of relations that you entertained in Busovaca? Did you have to go through him whenever you dealt with some military operations in Busovaca, for example? Was it possible for you to conclude from some of the military operations that he really did have command as far as the Busovaca area is concerned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I never called Mr. Kordic "Colonel". It was the first reference I've heard to him as "Colonel", which would make him equivalent rank, of course, anyway. But the answer to your question, Sir, I considered him to be the military commander de facto in Busovaca at the time I visited him in the evidence I've given, because he was the man -- you know, there are indications of someone being a military commander. An indication is that he sits in the operations room and is surrounded by a staff. An indication is that no one contradicts him. An indication is that when he gives instructions, they are generally carried out. An indication, indeed, is the fact he might disagree with someone who was the de facto military commander of Central Bosnia like Blaskic, and I've given evidence this morning as to that fact with regard to the landslide that was brought down on the Lasva Valley road. I'm not sure whether that's an answer, Sir. It's the best I can do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, in just a few minutes we'll go over each of the Orbats, the orders of battle that your regiment prepared in connection with the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, but are you telling us that you instructed your intelligence section that in your view, Mr. Kordic was, in fact, the military commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure I said that to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now turning to Mr. Kordic for just a second --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Did you say "Kordic" or "Blaskic" then? I'm sorry. Did you say that Mr. Kordic was the commander in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I asked you, sir, whether you had ever informed your intelligence section in the Cheshire Regiment, your milinfocell, that in your opinion Mr. Kordic was, in fact, the military commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I might have done, I might not have done. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with Mr. Kordic, let me just ask you a few general questions before we start going through the chronological material. Were you aware that there was an entity by the name of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that was in existence at the time of your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: A sort of political organisation, you mean? There are many phrases for it, HD -- whatever it is. Yes, I realised there was a political organisation. What it was called, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, and if you don't know, you don't know, and that's a perfectly fine answer. Were you aware that the HVO, the Croatia Defence Council, was separate from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, had a separate governance than people in positions of authority, and that those two entities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Before you start putting these matters, these may be matters which are in dispute and shouldn't be put as fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough, Your Honour. Let me lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask a more open-ended question, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Three entities that I would like to ask you to concentrate upon, Colonel. The first is the so-called HZ-HB or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which I've already discussed. Do you know who the president of that entity was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Not offhand. It was something to do with Valenta, I think, and others. They are all connected. This is the sort of Kordic line, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, do you know who the president of the Croatian Defence Council was when you first arrived in Bosnia in September of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the name Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I've heard of it, but beyond that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know who it is that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: You know, this was irrelevant to me. I was on the ground, trying to actually sort out a very chaotic situation. Who the hell was the president of an organisation which I didn't really understand, to be honest, was something I couldn't have the time to even think about. Forgive me, that sounds rude. I'm not trying to be. I'm just trying to say it was very difficult for me to try to concentrate on high-level stuff when I had enough problems already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that Mr. Valenta was, in fact, a vice-president of the HVO, having been appointed on the 17th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, but it comes as no surprise. I thought he was a vice-president of the organisation you've just described or the president, but very high ranking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kordic was never a vice-president or president of the HVO and that he never had any formal role within that organisation other than as a member of a committee on personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, again, is highly contentious. You're putting it as a fact. I don't think that we are going to advance much further. The witness has given his evidence as to what he knew about Kordic at the time. Now let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the third entity that I wanted to ask you some questions about, because there are several references to this in the milinfosums. Did you know that Mr. Kordic was one of five vice-presidents of the political party the HDZ-BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, I did. That's what he told me he was. Or that's what he said he was. Let's be factual. That's what he said he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a general question, sir. It would be fair to say that you were not aware of the distinctions between the HVO, the HZ-HB and the HDZ-BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The answer is I was aware that there was separate organisations. I personally felt they were very closely connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. There was a speech given by Mr. Kordic on November the 5th that's already been exhibited, Your Honours, Exhibit 129/1A, where Mr. Kordic is identified as the deputy president of Herceg-Bosna. Do you recall reading that speech at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like the usher to show you, if I may, milinfosum number 87, dated January the 26th, 1993, D106/1. I have one for the witness and one for the ELMO. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, if you would just turn to page 2, I would like to draw your attention to some observations made by the military intelligence section of your regiment in the middle of the page there regarding an incident in which certain mines were moved. And the comment is made by the military intelligence officer that Dario Kordic is the local representative for the HDZ, he claims to be the deputy to Mate Boban, and has considerable influence in the local area. Is that your understanding of what his position was as of January the 26th, 1993, the local representative of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Sounds fine by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you've previously stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you finished with that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It ought to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
